intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the gene encoding the neurofilament light chain polypeptide (NEFL) on chromosome 8p21.

checks.claim: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the NEFL gene, which encodes the neurofilament light chain polypeptide.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the neurofilament light chain gene (NEFL) cause early onset severe Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
checks.explanation: The paper supports NEFL mutations causing CMT, but the abstract does not use the term CMT1F or mention homozygous mutations or zygosity.

checks.claim: The NEFL gene is located on chromosome 8p21.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the NEFL gene were recently reported as a cause for autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2E (CMT2E) linked to chromosome 8p21.
checks.explanation: The abstract places NEFL-related disease at 8p21.

paragraphs.text: CMT1F is a hereditary peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the NEFL gene, which encodes the neurofilament light chain. It is characterized by early onset, often with a severe phenotype, and by moderately to severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. Jordanova et al. (2003) found that patients with NEFL missense mutations or an in-frame deletion had early onset and often severe disease. Both dominantly inherited forms, caused by missense mutations, and recessively inherited forms, caused by homozygous nonsense mutations, have been reported (Abe et al., 2009; Yum et al., 2009).

checks.claim: CMT1F is a hereditary peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the NEFL gene, which encodes the neurofilament light chain.
checks.evidence_quote: we screened 323 patients with CMT or related peripheral neuropathies. We detected six disease associated missense mutations and one 3-bp in-frame deletion
checks.explanation: The paper describes CMT caused by NEFL mutations but never uses the designation CMT1F.

checks.claim: CMT1F is characterized by early onset, often with a severe phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.

checks.claim: CMT1F is characterized by moderately to severely slowed nerve conduction velocities.
checks.evidence_quote: Electrophysiological examination shows moderately to severely slowed nerve conduction velocities.

checks.evidence_quote: We detected six disease associated missense mutations and one 3-bp in-frame deletion clustered in functionally defined domains of the NEFL protein. Patients have an early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype.

checks.evidence_quote: This is the first report of a homozygous nonsense mutation of NEFL. Results of our study show that nonsense NEFL mutations probably cause a recessive phenotype

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) noted that, by the conventional 38 m/s criterion, the neuropathy in their family with a homozygous NEFL mutation would be classified as demyelinating. However, they considered the absence of large myelinated axons the likely cause of the slowed conduction. They proposed the term 'severe, early-onset axonal neuropathy' (SEOAN) for the disorder. They also suggested that, under the OMIM convention, their patients should be designated CMT2B5.

paragraphs.text: Jordanova et al. (2003) screened 323 patients with CMT or related peripheral neuropathies and identified patients with NEFL mutations. These patients had early onset and often a severe clinical phenotype. Electrophysiologic examination showed moderately to severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. A nerve biopsy from a patient with a de novo NEFL missense mutation showed axonal pathology with axonal regeneration clusters and onion bulb formations.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) reported a 2-generation Palestinian family in which 4 of 5 children of consanguineous parents (first cousins) had CMT. The index patient presented at age 2 years with toe walking, and onset in all affected children was at about 1.5 years. All 4 affected individuals had hypotonia in infancy and early childhood, mildly delayed motor milestones, slowly progressive distal atrophy and weakness of the feet and hands, and bilateral pes cavus. At the time of the report, one patient used a walker and the others were ambulatory with molded ankle-foot orthoses. One patient had moderate proximal leg weakness and a waddling gait, and another had mild to moderate proximal arm and shoulder girdle weakness. All had moderate sensory impairment in a glove-and-stocking distribution and absent ankle jerks. CMT neuropathy scores ranged from 16 to 27. None had pathologic reflexes, palpably enlarged nerves, ulcerated feet, cranial neuropathies, or clinically evident hearing loss. One patient had learning difficulties, and the 3 patients who had brain MRI had normal scans.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) examined a sural nerve biopsy taken from 1 patient at age 16 years. It showed a myelinated axon density of 1,300/mm, compared with about 6,000/mm in controls. All myelinated axons were less than 3 microns in diameter and were often irregular in shape. There were occasional clusters of regenerated axons but no evidence of actively degenerating axons. Myelinated axons contained microtubules but no intermediate filaments. Immunostaining with an antiserum against the N terminus of NFL labeled axons, whereas an antiserum against the C terminus did not.

paragraphs.text: Abe et al. (2009) analyzed the NEFL gene in 223 Japanese CMT patients. Those with the demyelinating form had tested negative for mutations in PMP22, MPZ, GJB1, LITAF, EGR2, GDAP1, MTMR2, and PRX. Those with the axonal form had tested negative for mutations in MFN2, MPZ, GJB1, HSP27, HSP22, and GARS. They identified 4 heterozygous missense mutations in 5 unrelated patients: pro8-to-leu (P8L), glu90-to-lys (E90K), asn98-to-ser (N98S), and glu396-to-lys (E396K). In 1 other patient, they found a homozygous nonsense mutation, glu140-to-ter (E140X; -style numbering not given), which was the first reported homozygous nonsense mutation of NEFL.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected sibs from a consanguineous Palestinian family with CMT, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene by sequencing, predicted to result in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation, and the unaffected sib did not carry it. Sequencing of PMP22, GJB1, MPZ, EGR2, PRX, LMNA, GDAP1, and MFN2 in 1 or 2 patients showed no additional mutations, and PMP22 was neither duplicated nor deleted. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals analyzed at a diagnostic laboratory. In SW-13 vim- cells, the E210X mutant did not form an intermediate filament network, and it did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL. In SW-13 vim+ cells, which express vimentin, it did not interfere with the endogenous vimentin network. By contrast, the dominant Q333P mutant formed aggregates. The authors concluded that E210X causes a simple loss of function.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) noted that Nefl-null mice show no demonstrable axonal loss and that quiver quail, which are homozygous for a Q114X nonsense mutation in Nefl, show minimal pathology. This contrasted with the progressive axonal loss in their patients. The authors suggested the discrepancy may relate to the much greater length of human nerves and/or the longer human lifespan.

paragraphs.text: Abe et al. (2009) found a homozygous glu140-to-ter (E140X) nonsense mutation in the NEFL gene in 1 Japanese patient with CMT, the first reported homozygous nonsense mutation of NEFL. The patient was identified by NEFL screening of 223 Japanese CMT patients. The authors concluded that NEFL nonsense mutations probably cause a recessive phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected children of consanguineous Palestinian parents with severe early-onset CMT and slowed nerve conduction, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, resulting in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals tested at a diagnostic laboratory. In transfected SW-13 vim- cells, the mutant protein did not form filaments and did not interfere with filament assembly by wildtype NFL, consistent with a simple loss of function. A sural nerve biopsy from an affected patient showed reduced numbers of small myelinated axons that lacked intermediate filaments.

agent.process_note: Read all three papers in full: two were abstract-only (Jordanova 2003, Abe 2009), and Yum 2009 was full text. Checked variant details (c.628G>T/E210X; Glu140Stop; P8L, E90K, N98S, E396K), family structure, consanguinity, ages, NCV ranges and biopsy figures against the texts. The Jordanova abstract does not name its individual NEFL variants, so they are not listed as allelic variants. The Abe abstract does not say which missense carriers had demyelinating versus axonal CMT, so those missense variants are described only in Molecular Genetics. No NEFL MIM number was supplied in the reference data, so none is given; the chromosome location (8p21) is taken from the Jordanova abstract.
